findings.title: Async legacy writes run on the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
findings.body: The legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The request context is cancelled when the HTTP handler returns, which happens right after the unified-storage write completes. The legacy Create therefore almost always sees context.Canceled, the legacy copy is never written, and the only trace is a metric. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The detached goroutine should use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a background context) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Legacy write failures in mode 3 are counted but never logged
findings.body: In Create the goroutine stores the legacy error in errObjectSt and only records a duration metric; no log line is emitted. Update (line 140), Delete (line 113) and DeleteCollection (line 166) have the same gap. The previous synchronous code logged legacy failures. Since the async legacy write is now the only safety net, failures become invisible except as a counter with no object name or error text, so diverged objects cannot be identified.

findings.title: Delete passes the object name as the resource label on the storage duration metric
findings.body: recordStorageDuration is called with name where every other call passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new label value and a new time series that stays in the metrics registry for the life of the process. On a long-running server this grows metric cardinality and memory without bound.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded in the legacy duration metric
findings.body: In Create, when the unified-storage write fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage errors are counted against the legacy series and the storage error metric is not updated. Update (line 129) makes the same mistake. Dashboards and alerts comparing the two stores will report wrong numbers.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records legacy results under the storage metric
findings.body: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy results are counted as storage results, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection calls.

findings.title: Legacy create mutates the same object the storage write used, racing with the response
findings.body: The goroutine passes obj, the same pointer given to Storage.Create at line 42, to Legacy.Create while the handler continues to serialize the returned object. Legacy create paths typically assign UID, creationTimestamp and other metadata to the object in place. If the storage result shares memory with obj, this is an unsynchronized write concurrent with response encoding, and it can alter metadata of the object the storage already persisted. The goroutine should receive a deep copy (obj.DeepCopyObject()).

findings.title: Mode 3 update no longer sends the legacy store the object unified storage persisted
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo with the object produced by unified storage so that legacy stored exactly that result. Now the raw objInfo is passed to Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated again against the legacy store's own copy. For patch and apply requests the legacy result can differ from what unified stored. Any resourceVersion precondition is checked against the legacy RV, which differs from the unified RV, so legacy updates can fail with a conflict. Both outcomes are silent (see the logging finding), so the two stores can silently diverge.

findings.title: Delete puts the bare logger into the context, dropping name, kind and method
findings.body: Every other method stores the request-scoped log (with name, kind and method values) in ctx. Delete uses d.Log, so anything downstream that logs via klog.FromContext, including the storage Delete path, loses those key/values. This is inconsistent with the rest of the file.

findings.title: Dry-run requests are still dispatched to the legacy store
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection never check options.DryRun before spawning the legacy write. A dry-run request is meant to have no side effects. Unified storage honors it, but the legacy call is dispatched unconditionally with the same options, and this file does not rely on the legacy store honoring DryRun. The legacy goroutine should be skipped when len(options.DryRun) > 0.

findings.title: One unbounded goroutine per write, not tracked and not drained on shutdown
findings.body: Each successful write spawns a goroutine that holds the request object and options until the legacy call returns. There is no bound on in-flight legacy writes. Nothing waits for them on shutdown, and Destroy (line 172) calls Legacy.Destroy while those goroutines may still be using Legacy. A slow legacy store causes goroutines and retained objects to grow with the write rate.

findings.title: Update doc comment describes the old synchronous ordering
findings.body: The comment says Update writes first to Storage and then to LegacyStorage, which implies the legacy write is part of the synchronous call. It is now fire-and-forget in a goroutine and its errors are not returned. The Create comment (line 35) also does not say that the legacy write is asynchronous and best-effort, which callers need to know.

findings.title: Legacy writes in mode 3 are never verified by the tests
findings.body: Each success case sets up a legacy expectation (for example here), but nothing asserts that it was called: there is no AssertExpectations and no wait for the goroutine. Legacy and storage also share one mock object (lines 53-54 construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock with the same m), so a legacy call would satisfy a storage expectation with the same method name and arguments. A regression that never calls Legacy, or calls it with the wrong object, passes these tests. Since asynchronous legacy behavior is the point of mode 3, tests should wait for the legacy call and check it against a separate legacy mock.

findings.title: List test is named as 'not implemented' although List is implemented
findings.body: The case name says listing 'is not implemented', but this PR implements List by calling Storage.List. The case only checks that an error returned by the storage mock is propagated. The name should describe that, for example 'error when listing from the unified store fails'.

findings.title: New mode 3 subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes
findings.body: The new mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, which reads the legacy API right after k8s writes (getFromBothAPIs at lines 535 and 547, and later). With legacy writes now fire-and-forget, those reads race the goroutine and nothing waits for convergence. The subtests can be flaky, or fail deterministically if the legacy write fails (see the cancelled-context finding). The legacy-visibility checks should poll (for example with require.Eventually), or the test should document why these reads are unaffected in mode 3.

findings.title: go.work.sum gets unrelated checksum entries and a duplicated line
findings.body: The change adds checksums for modules unrelated to mode 3 (grafana-azure-sdk-go/v2, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporter and SDK versions, genproto rpc). This suggests a dependency tool was run and its output was committed. The github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery /go.mod line is also added even though an identical line already appears as context just above it, so it is duplicated. The unrelated lines should be reverted and the duplicate removed, or the PR should explain why they are needed.
